notes: \cpara{Recalls the previous day's post, ``Absolute Authority'' (8 January 2008), and quotes its point: certainty is a sufficient condition for choosing, not a necessary one.}
\cpara{Announces 2 + 2 = 4 as the subject, then discusses a physical law instead: the lightspeed limit may hold always and without exception. Arithmetic returns three paragraphs later.}
\cpara{States the distinction the post rests on: a claim can be exactly true while our confidence in it falls short of certainty.}
\cpara{Illustrates the distinction with a plagiarized assignment and an unseen coin, and states it in general form: a degree of uncertainty is not a degree of truth or a frequency of occurrence.}

\cpara{Extends the distinction to arithmetic, with hedges. Whether ``2 + 2 = 4'' is true in an abstract sense is ``questionable,'' and the post will ``guess'' that, in whatever sense it is true, it is exactly true.}
\cpara{Defends the guess: the statement is more credible than any philosophical account of what ``true'' means in it.}
\cpara{Applies the distinction to the post's own belief. Exact truth does not bring absolute confidence, because the evidence for 2 + 2 = 4 could have been hallucinated or misremembered.}

\cfact{Standard probability theory goes the other way for statements like the post's second example. It gives probability 1 to every logical truth: the \textsc{Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy} (``Bayesian Epistemology,'' 2022) says probabilism ``is often thought to demand that one be logically omniscient.'' That SS0 + SS0 = SSSS0 follows from the Peano axioms is a truth of that kind. Some Bayesians relax the demand for real reasoners (Hacking 1967; Garber 1983, as the entry reports). The post takes their side without saying that the standard theory requires probability 1 here.}

\cpara{Names the standard the post will use: calibration, in which statements given 99\% come true 99 times in 100. The question about a hundred people's thousand statements is answered two paragraphs later.}

\cpara{Declines to present the calibration experiments and points to the author's book chapter instead. The reason is the rule of ``Knowing About Biases Can Hurt People'' (4 April 2007): mention calibration only after warning about motivated skepticism. The notes on that post discuss the rule.}

\cpara{States the result without the evidence. The chapter cited in the previous paragraph supports it. It quotes a study by Fischhoff, Slovic and Lichtenstein (1977) in which people judged which of two causes of death was more frequent: ``Only 73\% of the answers assigned odds of 100:1 were correct,'' and at odds of a million to one or more, ``accuracy was 90\%.''}

\cpara{Translates 99.99\% into a count: 10,000 independent statements held with equal confidence, about one of them wrong. That follows from the calibration standard. The post allows that 2 + 2 = 4 might earn this level.}

\cpara{Offered as opinion (``I don't think''). The support is the difficulty of setting up 10,000 independent protocols, and an anecdote in footnote 2 that I could not check: the archived page would not load.}
\cpara{Heads off a misreading: 99\% confidence in ``2 + 2 = 4'' is confidence that it is always true, not a belief that it is true 99\% of the time.}

\cpara{The arithmetic holds: one statement every 20 seconds for 16 hours is 2,880 a day, so a million take about 347 days. The illustration repeats ``Absolute Authority'' of the day before: ``one million equally strong independent statements, one after the other, over the course of a solid year or so.''}

\cpara{Raises the count to a trillion. The time is understated by a factor of about a hundred. At the pace just given, a trillion statements take about 950,000 years, some twelve thousand lifetimes of eighty years. The slip makes the post's point look weaker than it is.}
\cpara{A joke. A googolplex is $10^{10^{100}}$.}

\cpara{In Knuth's arrow notation, 3 ↑↑↑ 3 is a tower of 3s whose height is $3^{27}$, about 7.6 trillion. The claim that such a confidence is not much closer to probability 1 than 90\% depends on a measure of distance the post does not give here. It comes the next day, in ``0 And 1 Are Not Probabilities'': on the log-odds scale every confidence short of 1 is infinitely far from 1.}
\cpara{A joke that applies the thesis to the sentence stating it. The next two lines say the author is not absolutely sure of it either.}

\cpara{The closing quotation gives a second argument against probability 1, and it is correct for updating by Bayes's rule. If $P(A)=1$, then $P(E)=P(E \mid A)$ for any evidence $E$, so $P(A \mid E) = P(E \mid A)P(A)/P(E) = 1$ whenever $P(E)>0$. No evidence can lower it. ``Absolute Authority'' had made the same point the day before: ``if it's theoretically possible for you to change your mind about something, it can't have a probability exactly equal to one.''}
